rationale: Adyen's docs show robust support for in-person card, chip, contactless, and mobile-wallet acceptance via PCI-certified terminals, Tap to Pay on iPhone, and Terminal API integration covering payments, refunds, tipping, and offline mode. One negative community anecdote cites past integration friction, but overall documentation strongly evidences the capability.

Adyen's Disputes API supports retrieving dispute data, accepting/defending disputes, and uploading defense documents, and webhooks provide async status updates that an agent could poll—enabling the basic building blocks for automated monitoring and evidence submission. However, there's no explicit mention of deadline-specific webhook events or any AI/agent drafting assistance for evidence responses.

Adyen's Management API supports ordering/registering terminals via API (adyen-pos-docs-11), and a general OpenAPI spec repo exists, but no evidence pack item describes an API endpoint for creating a 'location' entity itself. Community feedback also cites painful, lengthy integration for card-present/terminal provisioning, undercutting a smooth end-to-end story.

Adyen exposes APIs (Terminal API, Management API, Disputes API, webhooks, OpenAPI spec) and even an MCP server for LLM/agent access, plus payout configuration options, suggesting an agent could technically pull data and act on it. However, there's no direct evidence of a dedicated transactions/payouts reporting API or reconciliation feature tailored for automated ledger matching.

Direct probes confirm a working llms.txt (HTTP 200) and .md variants of docs pages, plus an official MCP server enabling LLM clients to interact with Adyen's platform via natural language—strong agent-oriented tooling despite lacking a discoverable OpenAPI spec at standard paths.

Evidence shows an MCP server enabling natural-language developer access to Adyen's APIs for building integrations, but no feature that surfaces AI-generated insights or suggestions from a merchant's transaction/payments data within the product.

Adyen exposes webhooks, a Management API, and an MCP server for natural-language/LLM integration, which could underpin automations, but there is no evidence of a dedicated feature for autonomous, persistent background automations—these are developer-facing building blocks rather than a turnkey agentic automation system.

Adyen offers an MCP server letting developers use natural language with an LLM client to build payment integrations faster, which shows some AI-native tooling, but this is a developer integration aid rather than a built-in assistant inside the POS product that end users can delegate operational tasks to.

The Terminal API and Management API use JSON/HTTP calls that can be automated and tested via a simulated testing system (docs-1, docs-11, docs-12, docs-28), suggesting some headless/CI-friendly automation of terminal management and payment flows. However, actual in-person payment capture inherently requires a physical terminal or device interaction, so it cannot be fully run headlessly end-to-end, and no CI-specific tooling or SDKs are mentioned.

The evidence only shows Adyen exposing an MCP server so external LLM clients can call Adyen's own tools (docs-13, docs-20, probe-4) — the reverse of the story, which asks for the product to consume external MCP servers' tools. There is no evidence Adyen In-Person Payments can plug in third-party MCP servers to extend its own capabilities.

Adyen documents an official MCP server enabling natural-language LLM client connections to its platform, confirmed both in docs and via probe of the dedicated mcp-server page, though no independent community validation exists.

Adyen offers an official MCP server that lets developers use natural language with an LLM client to connect to Adyen's platform and build integrations, but this is a developer-tooling capability for building solutions, not natural-language operation of the in-person payments product itself (terminals, refunds, tipping, etc. still require API/Customer Area interactions).
Evidence shows an MCP server and OpenAPI spec/GitHub repo for API integration, but there is no mention of an official CLI tool for Adyen In-Person Payments.

Adyen provides a documented Terminal/Management API, an OpenAPI spec repo, webhooks, and an official MCP server explicitly for LLM/agentic natural-language access, backed by machine-readable docs (llms.txt, .md pages) confirmed via probes. A community post notes integration friction with older POS protocols, but this doesn't negate the well-documented, agent-friendly API surface.

No evidence of scoped or least-privilege API credential/key management for agents; docs mention API keys/roles nowhere in the pack, only general integration, MCP server, and terminal management features.

Adyen provides an official OpenAPI specification repo and detailed Terminal API/POS docs plus an MCP server for LLM-assisted integration, but the docs themselves emphasize JSON messaging 'without the need for libraries' rather than dedicated official SDKs, and a community account describes a difficult, library-less integration (COM protocol) that led to abandoning the integration after hundreds of hours.

Adyen documents a general webhooks system for subscribing to asynchronous event notifications (payment outcomes, disputes, etc.), explicitly positioned to avoid polling — applicable to POS/Terminal API flows alongside other Adyen APIs. Evidence is docs-only with no hands-on POS-specific webhook confirmation, but the capability is clearly documented as a first-class integration mechanism.

Adyen publishes machine-readable OpenAPI specs (GitHub) and markdown docs accessible via .md endpoints and llms.txt, which supports some AI-native consumption, but there's no evidence of an interactive API console or runnable code examples—probes for a hosted OpenAPI/swagger endpoint returned 404s.

Adyen publishes a dedicated GitHub repository of API definitions in the OpenAPI Specification standard (including Terminal API used for in-person payments), providing machine-readable specs, even though the docs site itself does not serve a direct openapi.json endpoint.

Adyen documents a dedicated test Customer Area and test cards to simulate card brands, CVMs, and declines, plus a 'basic testing system to simulate transaction scenarios,' clearly enabling sandbox testing separate from production. However, this is not AI-native tailored (no explicit sandbox mode for MCP/agent workflows) and details on test-vs-production data isolation are thin.

The evidence shows Adyen has versioned API specs (OpenAPI repo) and various POS APIs, but there is no evidence of a documented deprecation policy or explicit API versioning practices for AI-native reliability needs.

Adyen exposes granular APIs (Management API, Terminal API, Disputes API) and an MCP server for natural-language/LLM-driven automation, which could be scripted to act on many items, but there is no documented native bulk/batch operation endpoint (e.g., bulk refunds, bulk terminal orders) in the evidence pack.

Adyen offers webhooks for asynchronous event notifications (payment outcomes, disputes) that developers can use to trigger custom downstream actions, but there is no evidence of a built-in rules/automation engine for defining conditional triggers—developers must write their own logic to consume webhook events.

No evidence of scheduling, recurring jobs, or workflow automation capabilities; the product is a POS/payments API with webhooks and an MCP server for natural-language interaction, but nothing about scheduled or recurring automated jobs.

No evidence of any automation versioning, review, or rollback capability; Adyen's in-person payments docs cover terminal integration, payments, refunds, and an MCP server for natural-language API access, but nothing about managing or rolling back automations.

Adyen's evidence pack is entirely about payment processing, terminal management, refunds, and tipping — there is no mention of item catalog management or inventory count synchronization across registers/channels. Adyen is a payments platform, not a POS/inventory system, but since catalog-receipts management could theoretically be an adjacent feature and no evidence supports it, this is 'none' rather than 'na'.

No evidence in the pack addresses digital or printed receipt issuance, receipt content/format, or card-network receipt requirements; the documentation covers terminals, payments, refunds, tipping, and disputes but never mentions receipts.

Adyen's Disputes API explicitly lets merchants retrieve dispute info, accept/defend disputes, and upload defense documents, and Adyen's webhook system generally supports async notifications, implying chargeback alerts are possible. However, the evidence pack lacks specifics on deadline tracking, automated chargeback notifications, or POS-specific dispute workflows, so support is inferred rather than fully detailed.

Adyen provides a unified Customer Area and Management API to order terminals to specific locations and manage terminals/transactions, implying some multi-location fleet capability, but there's no explicit documentation of per-location settings or per-location reporting breakdowns. A community account also describes painful, costly integration for card-present/omnichannel setups, casting doubt on ease of fleet operations.

Adyen documents a dedicated iOS mobile integration (Tap to Pay on iPhone SDK) for building payments into an app, but there is no equivalent Android mobile SDK evidence in the pack, and a community account describes painful, hundreds-of-hours integration efforts for card-present/POS solutions.

Adyen explicitly documents offline payments continuing when internet drops (docs-8) and markets terminals that 'stay up and running, even when the internet is down' (docs-25), implying store-and-forward. However, no evidence details the specifics of storage limits, forwarding reconciliation behavior, or hands-on validation of this feature working reliably in practice, and one community comment reflects frustration with card-present integration complexity generally.

Adyen exposes a Terminal API for payments, refunds, tipping, and a Management API for terminal ordering/config, plus a Disputes API and even an MCP server for natural-language API access, indicating broad API parity with UI features. However, some functions (terminal management, refunds) are explicitly also routed through the Customer Area UI, and a community account describes painful, incomplete card-present API integration ('made us integrate with COM... ditched Adyen'), showing real-world friction not reflected in the docs claims.

The evidence pack covers APIs, terminals, refunds, and disputes, but contains no mention of data export, data portability, or account closure/data-deletion tools that would let a merchant extract their transaction/customer data in open formats and leave the platform.

Adyen In-Person Payments is a closed commercial payments platform; there is no evidence of its source code (terminal firmware, POS integration engine, or core platform) being available under an open license. The only open-source artifact found is an OpenAPI spec repository (interface definitions), not the product's actual source code.

Adyen In-Person Payments is a proprietary, cloud-based payments platform requiring Adyen-supplied terminals and accounts managed via Adyen's hosted Customer Area; there is no evidence of any self-hostable core product, source availability, or on-prem deployment option.

Adyen documents a general webhooks system that avoids polling and delivers final outcomes for asynchronous processes, plus a separate Disputes API for retrieving/managing disputes, covering authorized/captured/refunded/disputed events conceptually. However, evidence is generic platform-level docs (not POS-specific webhook payloads for capture/refund lifecycle) and a community complaint highlights painful integration friction for card-present flows, so delivery is credible but with caveats.

Only a vague mention that merchants can 'change how you get paid' exists; there is no evidence of payout timing visibility, next-day/instant payout options, or any speed-up mechanism in the provided pack.

The evidence pack covers POS integration, terminal management, tipping, refunds, and MCP/webhooks, but contains no mention of data residency, regional data storage options, or configurable data location controls.
No evidence pack content addresses AI training data usage or opt-out controls; Adyen's in-person payments documentation covers integration, terminals, and payment flows only.

No evidence in the pack addresses data retention or deletion controls for Adyen In-Person Payments; the docs cover integration, terminals, refunds, and MCP but nothing on privacy/data lifecycle management.
No evidence in the pack addresses telemetry, usage tracking, or opt-out controls for AI-native users; documentation focuses on payment integration, terminals, and APIs.

Adyen docs claim a 'standalone terminal solution' for quick setup and Customer Area management of terminals, but the core integration model is API/JSON-based (Terminal API) requiring developer work, not a simple merchant self-serve pairing flow. A firsthand community account describes needing to integrate with Adyen's terminal architecture taking 'hundreds of hours,' directly contradicting the 'minutes' expectation for a merchant-ops user.

The evidence pack covers POS integration, terminals, refunds, tipping, and disputes, but contains no mention of reconciliation reports, itemized transaction/fee statements, or payout matching tools for merchant-ops.

Adyen advertises PCI PTS 6 certified terminals that handle card data via its Terminal API, which supports minimal PCI scope for card-present transactions, but the evidence pack contains no explicit vendor documentation outlining the developer's remaining PCI-DSS obligations (e.g., SAQ eligibility, scope-reduction guidance).

Adyen's Terminal API explicitly supports referenced and unreferenced refunds (full/partial) back to the original card, and refunds can also be issued from the Customer Area dashboard, covering API, POS, and dashboard channels as the story requires.

Adyen's Terminal API is well documented as a server-driven, JSON-based API for building custom POS checkouts (docs-17, docs-1, docs-2, plus refund/tipping/testing docs), and an OpenAPI spec exists on GitHub. However, a first-hand community account describes painful, hundred-hour integration efforts leading to abandoning Adyen for card-present, suggesting real-world friction not reflected in the docs.

Adyen docs explicitly describe a test Customer Area with an orderable Adyen test card supporting different card brands, CVMs, and declined payments, plus a 'basic testing system to simulate transaction scenarios' — directly matching the story. However, this is described as basic/limited rather than a full reader simulator, and community feedback describes friction and hundreds of hours integrating the card-present/terminal flow, suggesting real-world testing experience is more painful than docs imply.

No evidence in the pack addresses splitting a single sale across multiple payment methods or multiple payers; documentation covers tipping, refunds, offline payments, terminal management, etc., but nothing on split-tender or split-payer transactions.

Docs confirm terminals can be ordered via Customer Area or Management API and managed centrally, but there's no evidence describing a fast self-serve signup/approval flow for founders, and one community account describes a lengthy, hundreds-of-hours integration effort before abandoning Adyen, suggesting the 'same week' bar may not be typical.

Adyen's official docs explicitly describe a Tap to Pay on iPhone solution that lets merchants accept contactless payments directly on an iPhone without extra hardware, and marketing materials reiterate 'no extra hardware required.' Evidence is docs/marketing only (no independent hands-on confirmation), and only iPhone is mentioned, not Android.

Adyen's Management API supports ordering terminals via API and the Terminal API handles payment-terminal interactions, but broader fleet operations like device registration, status monitoring, and configuration updates are described as done through the Customer Area (a UI), not a full API surface. A community account also describes painful, hardware-protocol-heavy integration for card-present terminals, undercutting a smooth 'manage fleet via API' story.

Docs confirm tipping is supported and describe the flow (POS app sends a tip amount, shopper accepts/changes/declines on terminal), but there's no evidence of merchant-ops-configurable smart tip percentages or a UI for setting preset tip amounts—the feature appears developer/API-driven rather than a merchant-ops self-service configuration.

Square's documented Tap to Pay on iPhone and Terminal/Payments APIs explicitly support chip, contactless, and Apple Pay/Google Pay in-person payments, and community commentary corroborates its widespread use as a merchant card-present payment system.

Square offers a Disputes API (square-docs-11) and Webhooks (square-docs-12) that could support programmatic monitoring of dispute deadlines, plus an MCP server (square-docs-14) enabling agent-based interaction with the platform. However, there is no evidence of built-in AI drafting of evidence responses—developers would need to build that logic themselves on top of the raw API/webhook data.

Square's Locations API supports creating and managing locations via API (square-docs-9, square-docs-24), enabling that portion of the story. However, the evidence pack shows no Devices/Reader-registration API or documentation for programmatically registering hardware readers to a location, only Terminal API references to payment flows, so the 'registering readers' half of the story is unsupported.

Square exposes a documented Payouts API (list-payouts) and Payments/webhooks APIs via SDKs, and even offers an official MCP server for agent-based access to its platform, which directly supports an AI agent pulling transactions/payouts programmatically. However, there's no explicit evidence of a dedicated 'list transactions' or reconciliation-specific endpoint, and no confirmation that daily reconciliation into a ledger is a built-in workflow rather than something the agent must assemble from multiple APIs.

Square hosts a live llms.txt (HTTP 200) at developer.squareup.com/llms.txt describing its APIs/SDKs, and also documents an official MCP server for agent integration, directly satisfying the agent-oriented docs story despite lacking docs.md or openapi.json endpoints.

Square offers an official MCP server enabling AI agents/tools to query Square data, which could support external AI-generated insights, but there is no evidence of native, in-product AI-generated insights or suggestions (e.g., analytics recommendations) inside Square Dashboard itself.

Square offers webhooks, APIs, and an MCP server for integration, but there is no evidence of a background automation/workflow engine that runs autonomous tasks; the MCP server (square-docs-14) supports AI assistant tool access, not autonomous background automations.

Square offers an official Model Context Protocol (MCP) server enabling external AI agents/assistants to interact with Square's APIs, which supports agentic delegation, but there is no evidence of a native, built-in AI assistant embedded within the Square product/dashboard itself.

Square exposes full REST APIs, SDKs (e.g., Node.js), sandbox testing, and webhooks that can be scripted headlessly/in CI, plus a dedicated MCP server for AI agent integration. However, no direct evidence of a CLI, automated test harness, or CI-specific tooling/guides is present, and OpenAPI spec probes 404'd, suggesting limited machine-readable API discovery for full automation.

Square documents an official Model Context Protocol server (square-docs-14, square-probe-4), meaning Square itself acts as an MCP server exposing its tools—but this is the reverse direction of the story, which asks whether the product can consume/plug in external MCP servers as a client. There's no evidence Square's dashboard or product lets a user attach arbitrary MCP servers for it to use as an agent.

Square documents an official Model Context Protocol server (square-docs-14, square-probe-4), directly enabling AI agents to connect via MCP; llms.txt discoverability also supports agentic access (square-probe-1). No independent hands-on community validation of the MCP server's robustness is present, limiting confidence.

Square offers an official Model Context Protocol server (square-docs-14, square-probe-4) enabling AI agents/LLMs to interact with Square APIs via natural language, plus an llms.txt for AI discoverability (square-probe-1). However, there's no evidence of a native natural-language interface within Square's own dashboard/POS for everyday users—the MCP is a developer-facing integration tool, not a built-in NL command experience.

The evidence pack shows Square offers SDKs (e.g., TypeScript/Node.js library) and an official MCP server for AI agent integration, but there is no mention of an official command-line interface (CLuar) tool anywhere in the docs, GitHub, or probes.

Square offers extensive, well-documented public REST APIs covering payments, catalog, inventory, orders, disputes, payouts, locations, and webhooks, plus official SDKs (e.g., TypeScript/Node) and a sandbox for testing. It also has a dedicated Model Context Protocol (MCP) server and an llms.txt file, explicitly supporting AI-native/agentic consumption.

While Square offers an MCP server for agent integration and general API docs, the evidence pack contains no mention of scoped/least-privilege API credentials, OAuth permission scopes, or agent-specific access controls.

Square offers official SDKs (e.g., TypeScript/Node.js SDK on GitHub) with clear code examples, plus comprehensive API docs, sandbox testing, and even an official MCP server for AI agent integration, indicating strong support for building AI-native applications against official SDKs.

Square provides a documented Webhooks API/service (square-docs-12) with an overview and setup for subscribing to events, plus sandbox testing support (square-docs-13), confirming native webhook subscription capability for developers.

Square's developer docs list API references and a sandbox for testing, but there is no evidence of an interactive, runnable API reference (e.g., Swagger/OpenAPI explorer); explicit probes for openapi.json/swagger.json all returned 404s.

Square publishes a machine-readable spec via its open-source connect-api-specification repo (README referenced in square-docs-19), and offers an MCP server for agentic access, but direct standard endpoints like openapi.json/swagger.json on the main developer domain return 404 (square-probe-3), making discovery non-trivial.

Square provides a dedicated Sandbox environment with documentation ('Test in Sandbox') for testing API calls, payments, and webhooks without touching production data, and this is corroborated by SDK support and developer docs referencing sandbox usage across APIs.
The evidence pack shows extensive API documentation, SDKs, and even an MCP server, but none of the items reference API versioning schemes or a documented deprecation policy for Square's APIs.

The evidence pack shows Square's Catalog, Inventory, and Orders APIs plus an MCP server for AI integration, but none of the docs or community items explicitly describe bulk/batch operations across many items at once.

Square provides webhooks that fire on events (payments, orders, disputes) which developers can use to build automated rule-based reactions, plus an MCP server enabling AI-native tool integration, but there is no native rules/automation engine for defining trigger-action logic within Square itself—this requires external glue code.

Square provides webhooks, an MCP server, and APIs for payments/catalog/inventory, but there is no evidence of any scheduling primitive for recurring jobs or automated workflows (e.g., cron-like triggers, recurring invoices/subscriptions API, workflow automation engine) in the evidence pack.

Square's evidence covers payments, catalog, inventory, and an MCP server for API access, but there is no mention of versioning, reviewing, or rolling back automations—no workflow/automation builder with history or rollback exists in the pack.

Square provides a dedicated Catalog API and Inventory API for managing items and stock levels, plus a Locations API supporting multi-location sellers, and marketing copy explicitly touts 'Track inventory' and 'Manage orders from one place' across the business — indicating catalog/inventory sync across registers and channels is a core supported capability.

Square supports customizable receipt text per location (custom_receipt_text field for disclaimers/promos) and its Terminal/Payments APIs imply receipt issuance, but the evidence pack lacks explicit documentation of email/SMS digital receipt delivery or explicit card-network compliance requirements for receipts.

Square has a documented Disputes API (square-docs-11) supporting programmatic processing of disputes, and Webhooks (square-docs-12) that could notify merchants of dispute events, implying the capability exists. However, there is no direct evidence of dashboard notifications, deadline tracking, or evidence-submission UI/workflow, nor community confirmation of this specific flow, so delivery is only partially substantiated.

Square's Locations API explicitly supports multiple locations per account (created beyond the default single location) with per-location settings like custom receipt text, and Dashboard lets sellers review/edit location info. However, evidence lacks detail on per-location device management or per-location reporting depth, so support for a full multi-location hardware fleet workflow is only partially substantiated.

Square provides an official Mobile Payments SDK for iOS and Android (square-docs-4) with Tap to Pay on iPhone support (square-docs-2) and offline payments handling (square-docs-5), directly enabling developers to embed in-person card payments into custom mobile apps.

Square documents an explicit 'Offline Payments' feature in the Mobile Payments SDK for Android, indicating support for storing and forwarding transactions when connectivity drops, but this is scoped to a specific SDK/platform rather than a universal guarantee across all Square hardware (Terminal, POS, Tap to Pay), and no community evidence confirms real-world reliability of this offline flow.

Square exposes broad APIs covering payments, catalog, inventory, locations, orders, disputes, payouts, webhooks, sandbox, and even an MCP server for AI agents, suggesting most core UI workflows are API-accessible. However, no evidence of a full OpenAPI spec (probes 404'd) or confirmation that every dashboard feature (e.g., payroll, team scheduling) is fully API-parity, leaving gaps for a true 'everything via API' claim.

Square provides APIs (Catalog, Inventory, Orders, Locations, Payouts) that allow programmatic data retrieval in JSON via REST/SDKs, giving some data portability, but there's no evidence of a bulk 'export all my data' feature or open-standard full account export; OpenAPI spec probes returned 404s, suggesting limited machine-readable schema discoverability.

Square is a closed-source SaaS platform; while its SDKs (e.g., square-nodejs-sdk) are open source, the core product/source code is proprietary and not available under an open license. No evidence indicates the platform's source itself can be read openly.
Square is a cloud-based payments/commerce SaaS platform with no self-hostable core product; the self-hosting axis does not apply to this type of service.

Square documents a dedicated Webhooks system (square-docs-12) and a Disputes API (square-docs-11) that could feed dispute-related events, indicating webhook support for payment lifecycle events. However, the evidence pack lacks explicit detail on specific event types (authorized, captured, refunded) or examples of subscribing to them, so full coverage isn't confirmed.

Square provides a Payouts API (List Payouts) to check payout status/timing, and Square's dashboard is known to offer instant/next-day transfer options, but the evidence pack has no explicit documentation of instant vs next-day payout speed configuration or scheduling, only a generic 'List Payouts' endpoint and a 'Manage your cash flow' marketing blurb.

No evidence in the pack addresses data residency, regional storage options, or compliance controls for choosing where data is stored; Square's docs focus on payments, catalog, inventory, and developer SDKs.
No evidence pack items address AI training data usage, opt-out policies, or privacy controls related to AI model training; Square's evidence is entirely about payments, commerce APIs, and hardware.

The evidence pack covers Square's payments, catalog, orders, and developer APIs but contains no mention of AI data retention, deletion controls, or privacy settings for AI-native usage such as an MCP server.
No evidence in the pack addresses telemetry opt-out or usage tracking controls for AI-native or developer users of Square's products or APIs.

Square documents Tap to Pay on iPhone and hardware/Terminal API support for taking payments quickly, and community comments confirm the reader-based checkout model is fast and functional, but there is no direct evidence describing the reader pairing/registration setup flow or its actual time-to-first-payment experience.

Square provides a Payouts API to list payouts and general transaction/order/catalog APIs that could support reconciliation, but there is no direct evidence of itemized fee reports or a dedicated reconciliation report combining takings vs payouts. No community or docs evidence explicitly confirms this workflow is well-supported for merchant-ops reconciliation.

Square's certified hardware (Tap to Pay, Terminal API) and tokenized payment APIs (sourceId in payments.create) suggest card data is captured by certified devices and not touched directly by developer code, reducing PCI scope. However, the evidence pack contains no explicit PCI-DSS scope guidance, SAQ eligibility documentation, or compliance certification details from Square for developers.

The evidence pack includes docs on payments, disputes, and catalog/inventory APIs, but no citation describes a Refunds API, POS refund flow, or dashboard refund capability for full/partial refunds to original card.

Square provides a documented Terminal API for driving card-present checkout flows (tip screens, custom amounts) plus SDKs, sandbox testing, webhooks, and orders/catalog APIs to build a full custom POS backend integration.

Square provides a Sandbox for testing (square-docs-13) and Terminal API docs for in-person payment flows (square-docs-26), but the evidence doesn't specifically confirm a simulated physical reader or test card environment tailored to in-person/Terminal integrations, leaving gaps for full end-to-end in-person testing confidence.

No evidence in the pack addresses split-tender or multi-payer transaction splitting; docs cover payments, catalog, inventory, disputes, but nothing on splitting a single sale across multiple payment methods or payers.

Evidence confirms Square offers self-serve sign-up, hardware/Tap to Pay options, and dashboard-based location/account management, consistent with a fast onboarding flow, but there is no direct evidence of approval speed, hardware ordering/shipping timelines, or same-week readiness claims in the pack.

Square explicitly offers Tap to Pay on iPhone, letting merchants accept contactless cards, Apple Pay, and other wallets directly on an off-the-shelf iPhone with no extra reader hardware, documented both as a consumer feature and as a developer SDK.

Evidence shows a Terminal API for checkout/tip flows (square-docs-26) but nothing about registering devices, monitoring device status, or remotely updating configuration for a fleet of readers/terminals — no Devices API or fleet-management endpoints are cited.

Square's Terminal API docs confirm tip collection with a separate tip input screen and custom tip amounts, supporting the core capability, but evidence is developer-API focused rather than showing merchant-ops-facing configuration of preset percentages or smart amounts in a dashboard/reader settings UI.

Docs confirm chip/contactless card reader support, Tap to Pay on iPhone/Android for contactless, and mobile-wallet acceptance via readers, plus fleet management, offline mode, and receipts—corroborated by community reports of real-world merchant deployments using Stripe Terminal for in-person payments.

Stripe provides generic webhooks (docs-38) and a Dispute automation feature 'Smart Disputes' that automates evidence collection/submission (docs-40), plus platform-level AI agent tooling via MCP (docs-35, docs-36), which together could support an agent monitoring disputes and drafting responses. However, none of this is Terminal-specific, there's no explicit dispute-deadline webhook event or agent-draft-for-review workflow documented, only generic dashboard automation.

Stripe Terminal exposes API-based location and zone management and reader registration (by registration code, serial number, or order number) that can be done fully via API without physical possession, meeting end-to-end programmatic provisioning needs; Stripe also provides an official MCP server and OpenAPI spec enabling agent-driven API calls.

Stripe's platform (which Terminal transactions flow through) exposes payouts and balance data via API (docs-39), webhooks for event-driven sync (docs-38), and an official MCP server letting AI agents call the Stripe API (docs-35), giving the building blocks for an agent to pull transactions/payouts and reconcile them. However, there's no Terminal-specific reconciliation or ledger feature, and no evidence of a purpose-built agent workflow for daily reconciliation, so support is generic/indirect rather than a dedicated capability.

Stripe hosts a working llms.txt (probe returns HTTP 200) and .md versions of docs pages (confirmed by probe and used throughout the evidence pack), plus dedicated agent-oriented docs like docs.stripe.com/agents.md and an MCP server for AI agents to query Stripe's API and knowledge base.

Stripe Terminal's evidence covers payment hardware, reader management, receipts, tipping, and offline support, but shows no AI-generated insights or suggestions surfaced from transaction/business data within the product itself. The MCP/agent tooling ([stripe-terminal-docs-35],[stripe-terminal-docs-36]) is generic Stripe platform infrastructure for building agents, not an in-product analytics/insights feature for Terminal users.

Stripe Terminal is a point-of-sale hardware/SDK product for in-person payments; the evidence shows webhooks, MCP, and CLI exist at the broader Stripe platform level, but nothing indicates Terminal itself supports autonomous background automations tied to its POS/reader workflows.

Stripe Terminal is a hardware/SDK payment product with no built-in AI assistant inside the product; the only AI-related evidence is Stripe's platform-wide MCP server and 'Agents' developer tooling for building agent integrations, not a delegated in-product assistant for Terminal itself.

Terminal offers an API-based integration and a built-in simulated card reader for testing without physical hardware, plus the Stripe CLI for terminal-based automation, which supports some headless/CI development workflows. However, actual payment processing fundamentally requires a physical reader, so full headless production automation isn't supported—only testing/dev automation is evidenced.

Evidence shows Stripe exposes its own MCP server so AI agents can call the Stripe API (docs-35), but there is no evidence that Stripe Terminal itself acts as an MCP client/host capable of plugging in and using external MCP servers' tools.

Stripe (the parent platform) provides an official MCP server letting AI agents interact with the Stripe API and knowledge base, but this is a Stripe-wide capability, not something specific to or documented for Terminal (in-person payments) workflows—no evidence Terminal-specific actions (reader management, in-person payment flows) are exposed via MCP tools.

Stripe provides a platform-wide MCP server letting AI agents interact with the Stripe API and docs, which could technically extend to Terminal's API-based reader operations, but there is no Terminal-specific evidence of natural-language control over reader/POS actions like registering readers, collecting tips, or issuing refunds.

Stripe provides an official CLI ('Stripe CLI helps you build, test, and manage your Stripe integration right from the terminal') documented at docs.stripe.com/cli and docs.stripe.com/stripe-cli, applicable to Terminal integrations as part of the broader Stripe platform.

Stripe Terminal exposes a fully documented API-based integration path alongside SDKs, backed by a public OpenAPI spec, CLI, and webhooks, and is explicitly supported by Stripe's MCP server enabling AI agents to interact with the Stripe API.
